Hi everyone! 👋

I'm an enthusiastic and motivated participant in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. I'm interested in technology, innovation, problem-solving, AI, data science, and space exploration.

I'm particularly interested in using NASA Earth observation data to solve real-world problems, especially in agriculture, climate change, and environmental sustainability.

For this challenge, I would love to work on Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data, developing an innovative solution
summary:
AgriSense Ethiopia is a mobile and web app that turns NASA satellite data into simple, practical farming decisions for smallholder farmers in Ethiopia and across Africa. Farmers register their farm on a map, and AgriSense uses NASA Earth observation data (vegetation health from MODIS NDVI, rainfall from GPM IMERG, soil moisture from SMAP, and temperature from NASA POWER) to show crop health, climate trends and drought risk. An AI advisor answers questions such as “Is my farm at risk of drought?” and gives clear actions with a confidence level, while alerts warn farmers about drought or heavy rain before they happen.

This directly answers the FieldShift challenge by using NASA open data as the core of how farms adapt to a changing climate. It matters because most African farmers depend on rain and make decisions without evidence. AgriSense helps them save water, protect crops and raise productivity, and it can scale to any region because NASA data covers the whole continent.
details: AgriSense Ethiopia is an app that helps smallholder farmers use NASA satellite data without needing technical skills. A farmer signs up, chooses a role (farmer, agricultural expert, researcher or cooperative), and draws their farm on a map, adding the crop, farm size and planting date. The app then uses NASA Earth observation data to show vegetation health (NDVI, from MODIS), rainfall (GPM IMERG), soil moisture (SMAP) and temperature (NASA POWER). The data is turned into a dashboard, a satellite vegetation map, climate trends and a drought risk level. An AI advisor answers questions like “Is my farm at risk of drought?” and gives clear actions with a confidence level. Alerts warn the farmer about drought, crop stress or heavy rain, and reports can be exported as PDF. Benefits and intended impact Farmers can decide when to plant and water using evidence instead of guesswork. This helps them save water, protect crops, prepare for climate risks and raise productivity and income. We want to start with maize farmers in Ethiopia and then scale to cooperatives and other African countries, because NASA data covers the whole continent and is free and open. Tools and technology [Edit this part to match what you really used, for example: Figma or another design tool for the UI prototype; React, Flutter or HTML/CSS/JavaScript for the app; Python for data processing; NASA Earthdata and the datasets above for data; GitHub for code.] The NASA datasets we use are MODIS NDVI, GPM IMERG, SMAP and NASA POWER. Creativity Most climate and satellite tools are made for scientists. AgriSense brings NASA data to the farmer’s level: a map-based setup, plain-language advice, and a conversational AI advisor that is honest about its confidence. We designed the whole experience around one real farmer, Sami. Factors we considered Simplicity: screens that a first-time smartphone user can understand. Trust: AI advice shows a confidence level so farmers know how much to rely on it. Access: we plan SMS and voice support for farmers with basic phones. Language: we plan Amharic and Afaan Oromo support. Scale: open NASA data keeps costs low.
